subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Availability Cascade
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Availability Cascade.

hook.text: A rare plane crash dominates the news for weeks. Suddenly everyone thinks flying is dangerous. It's not.

buildup.text: An availability cascade starts with a vivid event, then media coverage makes it seem common and important.

discovery.text: Public concern grows, which triggers more coverage, which triggers more concern. A self-feeding loop.

twist.text: The real risks—heart disease, car crashes, air pollution—kill quietly and steadily. They don't go viral.

climax.text: Policy shaped by cascades misallocates resources: solving dramatic problems while ignoring deadly ones.

punchline.text: What you hear most isn't what matters most.

quiz.question: What drives an availability cascade?
options: A feedback loop between media coverage and public concern

details.summary: An availability cascade is a self-reinforcing process where a belief gains credibility through repetition in public discourse. The more people talk about something, the more available it becomes in memory, making it seem more true and important, which generates even more discussion.
details.whyItMatters: Availability cascades explain how minor risks get blown out of proportion and how misinformation spreads. Volume of discussion is not evidence of truth.
takeaways: Repetition increases perceived truth and importance
Media coverage creates self-reinforcing belief cycles
Frequency of discussion is not evidence of accuracy

faq.question: How does an availability cascade start?
faq.answer: A striking or emotionally compelling claim gets initial attention. Media covers it, making it more available in public memory. People discuss it, convincing others of its importance. Experts who challenge it get drowned out by volume.

faq.question: What is a real example of an availability cascade?
faq.answer: Shark attack fears spike every summer despite the minuscule statistical risk. One dramatic attack gets massive media coverage. People discuss it. Media covers the story more. Suddenly sharks feel like a major threat, even though you are far more likely to be harmed by a vending machine.
